name: Alignment
description: Learn how base, posture, and structure work together in BJJ. Preserve your own alignment and disrupt your opponent’s across positions, transitions, and submissions.
summary: Alignment coordinates base, posture, and limb structure so you can direct force and move effectively. Preserve or recover your own alignment while disrupting the opponent’s, regardless of position or role.
overview: Alignment brings base, posture, and structure together into one practical question: can you move and direct force toward your goal without giving the opponent easy control? A recognizable position does not guarantee useful alignment. You can be on top but off balance, or underneath with strong frames and a clear route to recovery. During a transition, the relationship between your support points, spine, and limbs matters more than holding a fixed shape. During a submission exchange, the attacker tries to separate these supports while the defender reconnects them. Assess both players before committing, and improve the missing part instead of compensating with more effort.
key_principles: Maintain support points that let you resist and generate force
Keep head, spine, and pelvis organized for the intended movement
Connect limbs to your torso rather than reaching without support
Disrupt the opponent’s alignment before demanding a large movement
Reassess alignment while changing grips and positions
Recover structure and posture before escalating effort

component_skills.description: Locate the support points that let you move without collapsing or overcommitting.
Check whether your head, spine, and hips support the direction you intend to move.
Identify unsupported limbs and reconnect them to useful frames or control points.
Notice which of the opponent’s base, posture, or limb structure is easiest to disrupt.
Restore one useful support at a time while preserving the others under pressure.

principle_relationships.description: Base supports the mechanics described in Alignment; apply both when assessing each player’s control and recovery options.

application_contexts.how_applied: Move the opponent beyond a useful support point before committing to a takedown.
Keep frames connected to the hips while disrupting the passer’s posture.
Direct weight through stable supports without reaching past your base.
Restore a frame and useful spinal alignment before turning into space.
Control alignment around the target; on defense, reconnect the limb and recover movement.

decision_framework.decision_point: Can you act without losing structure?
decision_framework.action: Disrupt the opponent’s alignment before demanding a large movement

common_errors.consequence: A top position can still be mechanically weak.
common_errors.correction: Check support, spine, and limbs before advancing.
Adjust alignment as the force direction changes.

common_errors.consequence: The opponent can separate the limb from the torso.
common_errors.correction: Move your base before extending your reach.

common_errors.consequence: Strong frames fail if posture or base collapses.

common_errors.error: Using effort to hide a gap
common_errors.correction: Recover the missing support before adding force.

training_approaches.description: Pause a cooperative exchange and identify each player’s base, posture, and structure.
Begin with one compromised support and recover it against light resistance.
Change positions slowly and pause when alignment deteriorates.
Score a point for disrupting alignment and stabilizing before advancing.

observable_behaviors: Names the relevant supports in a paused exchange
Demonstrates the principle with a cooperative partner
Recognizes when control is lost and resets
Uses the principle against light resistance
Explains both the attacking and defensive application
Recovers the relevant structure after one disruption
Maintains the principle through changing positions
Adapts when the opponent blocks the first route
Combines the principle with timing and angle changes
Diagnoses subtle failures under varied resistance
Chooses when to release or replace a connection
Teaches the principle using examples from multiple roles
